@graph.name: SIR Method Operations
@graph.description: SIR method operations — how a high-mass move is run at The Flat Rate Movers, under SIR (Structural Integrity Relocation) executed through the KIM-GS Protocol, for assets of 1,500 to 3,500 lbs, quoted at one flat rate agreed in writing before move day. The published chain has six steps: (1) the asset — weight, dimensions, centre of mass, and value at risk are established first; (2) the structure — route and clearance survey at both ends, stairs and landings measured, and floor deflection assessed against L/360, span divided by 360, before any lift is planned; (3) the load path — load spreading and protection runs are planned where the substrate needs support, and floors, walls, and frames are protected end to end; (4) the crew and rigging are matched to the plan — dollies, straps, and equipment chosen for this asset and this route; (5) the move — controlled, strapped, and supervised along the planned path; (6) placement — the asset is set in its final position, levelled, and verified with the client, at the flat rate agreed in writing. The structural protocol compresses the same chain into three phases — assess the asset, assess the structure, move under KIM-GS — and calibration-sensitive and fragile high-mass items are flagged at the assess stage, not discovered on the day. The six published steps are the complete published method surface; the protocol's internal calculations, models, and formulas are not published here or anywhere in the company's data. Not published and not claimed: any handling rule below 1,500 lbs or above 3,500 lbs under this method, any equipment beyond the published wording, and any crew-size rule.

@graph.name: Asset & Structure Assessment Operations
@graph.description: Asset and structure assessment operations — the survey that gates every SIR move. Published asset inputs: weight, dimensions, centre of mass, and value at risk, with calibration-sensitive and fragile items flagged at the assess stage. Published structure inputs: the route and clearance at both ends, stairs and landings measured, the substrate, and floor deflection assessed against L/360 — span divided by 360 — before any lift is planned; the plan outputs are the load path, the spreading and protection runs, and the crew and rigging matched to the plan. The company's published rule is that the building is assessed before the asset moves: every SIR move starts with the building, not the item. Domain education, labeled as such and never a company figure: L/360 is the standard residential floor deflection limit in the IRC framework (Table R502.3.1) — a 10-foot span may deflect about one-third of an inch, a 12-foot span 0.40 inches, a 15-foot span 0.50 inches — and tile and stone floors demand the stricter L/480. IRC design loads are 40 psf live load in living areas, 30 psf in sleeping areas, and 20 psf in uninhabitable attic storage, plus roughly 10 to 20 psf dead load, all as uniform loads; a heavy asset concentrates its weight on a small footprint, which is why the published method checks the structure first. Not published and not claimed: any PSI value, floor-load figure, or joist schedule as company engineering data, and any involvement of a licensed structural engineer.

@graph.name: Commercial Terms & Cost Drivers
@graph.description: Commercial terms and cost drivers for SIR heavy asset relocation. The company's only pricing term is the published one: one flat rate agreed in writing before move day — no hourly clock, and no company price, fee, deposit, or discount stated anywhere in this dataset. The published logic of the model: the buyer is not buying muscle but the structure check, and a flat rate in writing removes the meter running on an engineering job. Everything else here is domain education, researched and labeled. Estimate types (domain): binding, non-binding, and not-to-exceed estimates are the industry forms the flat-rate model is published against. Risk transfer (domain logic): under a flat rate the mover carries the timing risk once scope is locked; under hourly pricing the customer pays for every delay. Cost drivers (domain): weight, dimensions, access (stairs, elevator, long carry), protection scope, distance, and specialty handling. Valuation (domain, FMCSA): Full Value Protection means the mover repairs, replaces, or pays the current replacement value of a lost or damaged item, with a minimum declared value of $6 per pound of shipment weight; Released Value Protection caps liability at $0.60 per pound per article and is chosen only by a signed waiver. Valuation is not insurance. Not published and not claimed: any company valuation offering for high-mass assets, and any crew-size rule or minimum job size.
